argument_summary: Certification is supportable only as a narrow, caveated decision on the current admissible record. The strongest support is that aggregate launch readiness clears target by 2.5 percentage points and the launch rehearsal had no severity-one incidents. That support is limited, not clean: the developer-support migration segment misses target by 1.1 percentage points, that segment is named in a partner launch checklist, and legal review on disclosure remains open. The appropriate treatment is not to recast the gap as resolved or immaterial, but to treat certification as qualified by explicit residual-risk notation and continued monitoring.
claims_about_business_cost: No independent business-cost claim is needed to justify the packet. Remaining uncertainty can be handled through a bounded caveat and monitoring rather than escalation, because the admissible operational record shows aggregate readiness above threshold and no severity-one rehearsal incidents.
claims_about_policy: The admissible policy record cuts both ways. Public governance guidance supports documenting limitations and evaluation results and managing residual risk through ongoing measurement and monitoring. But the internal policy text says a weakness is material if it affects a named launch use case, and product labels such as non-core or low-volume do not resolve materiality when the affected segment is named or legal review is pending. On this record, policy does not support a clean no-disclosure merits claim; it supports, at most, a constrained certification packet that expressly acknowledges the unresolved disclosure and materiality question.
concessions: The named-segment evaluation gap is unresolved on the present record.
The partner-checklist reference weakens any argument that the affected segment is simply non-core.
The open legal review means the disclosure question is not closed.
The current record does not support claiming the gap is immaterial or fully covered by policy.
